newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE-Filmstar takes on cleric in Pakistan poll.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Filmstar takes on cleric in Pakistan poll.

text.p: In one of the oddest contests in Monday's Pakistani elections, singing and dancing screen idol Mussarat Shaheen is taking on a Moslem cleric in a conservative constituency.
Shaheen said she decided to stand as an independent against Maulana Fazlur Rehman in this North West Frontier Province town because she was saddened by its lack of progress.
"This is my ancestral constituency. Conditions in the area are very bad. The world is going into the 21st century but here it is going backwards," she told Reuters.
FATHER'S MANTLE

Rehman is unworried. He has won a National Assembly (lower house) seat from Dera Ismail Khan twice as head of his own faction of the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam (JUI) since inheriting his father's political mantle.
Besides Shaheen, he also faces a candidate from the new Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) of former Pakistani cricket star Imran Khan, a national hero who is from the region.

Rehman said his only serious challenger was the candidate of former prime minister Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Moslem League (PML), which is widely expected to emerge from the elections as the biggest party in the 217-seat National Assembly.
FOREIGN MEDIA

"Imran Khan and Mussarat Shaheen have been propagated by the foreign media. There is nothing on the ground. The people of this constituency are religious-minded people who do not like such things," he said.
Nisar Ali, a street vendor in the central market, backed that view, saying the sultry siren was part of an industry where morals were lax.
But Shaheen's campaign manager, former Rehman backer Pir Sabir Shah, said she was hoping to capitalise on a perceived popular reaction against the main parties.
Former prime minister Benazir Bhutto was dismissed on disputed corruption charges in November and the PML was also accused of graft when it was last in power.
"Mussarat urges the people to discard the traditional politicians and vote her to power," said Shah.
He said she could also exploit anger against the maulanas, or Moslem clerics, who are highly influential among the poor.
"Mussarat can get the anti-maulana vote. Hatred against maulanas exists amongst the people of this constituency," he said.
Rehman is supported by Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) -- and some say that could cost him votes.

"Fazlur Rehman has digressed from his mission. We have been fighting against the PPP for years and now he has joined hands with Benazir. He has betrayed our confidence," said Rab Nawaz, a bearded hotel caretaker.
REHMAN UNFAZED
Rehman said he was not worried about that, either.

"There is propaganda against me because JUI is a religious party that is popular with the people," he said. "The Western powers are afraid of JUI and that is why they want to distort the leader so as to break the party."
"There is a perception that people are against me because I have joined Benazir, but this has no value," he said.
Shaheen has drawn hundreds of people to her rallies and has impressed many with a seasoned style. But most think she is unlikely to win.
"The actual contest is between Fazlur Rehman and (the PML's) Umer Farooq," said Gohar Majeed, an auto spare-parts shop owner.
"Mussarat will get a few votes from the city where people watch her movies or from the taxi-drivers who are her fans."
